There was a time, within living memory, when Australian Christianity had a definable and active left wing: Palm Sunday peace marches, guitar masses, priests coming home from far-flung missions with stories of liberation theology and, in the early 2000s, powerful and sustained activism against government policies of mandatory detention.

items.title: Pope Leo says there is no change to agenda or priorities after his lung cancer surgery
items.summary:
ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE — Pope Leo XIV said his recent lung cancer surgery has not altered his agenda, outlook or even sense of mortality, as he projected a long pontificate focused on unity and healing within the church.

Leo seemed full of health, energy and jokes during an airborne news conference on Monday while returning to Rome from Peru. The grueling, 12-day trip through three South American countries left several members of the travelling Vatican delegation and press corps sick.

“I’m not 100 percent but I’m pretty good,” Leo said of his surgical recovery. “Endurance is one of the gifts the Lord gave me.”

Leo, 71, had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13 because of a cancerous tumor. He said it was discovered by chance during an annual checkup and appeared at first as a shadow on his lung.

“The first news was a surprise. There were no symptoms. I felt fine,” he said. Once the cancer was confirmed, he decided to proceed immediately to have it removed, and said he hoped his experience would help others not fear having checkups or pursue preventive care.

Leo saw no need for the provisional letter of resignation 

Prior to going into surgery, Leo said he saw no need to make provisions for the leadership of the Catholic Church if he were left medically impaired and unable to govern.

He said he hadn’t written any instructions, as his predecessors had done, outlining the criteria under which he would resign, which some legal experts believe is necessary if a pope were to end up in an irreversible coma and unable to articulate his resignation.

“Eventually I…
items.t: Pope Leo says there is no change to agenda or priorities after his lung cancer surgery

items.title: US Catholic bishops meet after Democrats’ big wins help reshape immigration and abortion debates
items.summary:
U.S. Catholic bishops are holding their annual fall meeting in Baltimore this week. The gathering comes just after Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories reset the political dynamics around some of the bishops’ priorities, including immigration, abortion and artificial intelligence.

The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops is now facing a divided government as it seeks to influence both the faithful and public policy.

“Midterm elections are the opportunity for people to assess where we are as a country and where we hope to go,” said Bishop Michael Burbidge of Arlington, Virginia. “I think what the citizens are asking — and we’re certainly praying for — is that those who are elected will be devoted to doing all that is right and just and true and somehow find a way to begin working together and addressing the issues that impact individuals and families.”

Catholics overall are politically mixed. Catholic voters split roughly evenly between Republican and Democratic candidates for the U.S. House, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters.

There was a split between white Catholics and Latino Catholics: Just over half of white Catholics supported the Republican House candidate in their area, while about two-thirds of Latino Catholics supported the Democratic House candidate in their area.

Nationally, just over half of Catholics said the Trump administration’s actions on immigration enforcement had “gone too far,” according to The AP Voter Poll. A similar share disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement was doing its job.

During…
items.t: US Catholic bishops meet after Democrats’ big wins help reshape immigration and abortion debates

items.title: Pope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in Peru
items.summary:
ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE — Pope Leo XIV has forgiven the person who threw a rosary at him before his final Mass in Peru and nailed him in the eye, saying it was merely a sign of the person’s profound faith.

Leo got hit during a popemobile ride Monday through the estimated 1.5 million people who had flooded a Lima air base for the service. Leo grimaced and touched his eye but proceeded as if nothing had happened.

During an in-flight press conference en route home, a Peruvian reporter apologized for the incident. Leo, who lived in Peru for two decades and has Peruvian citizenship, brushed it off as merely someone trying to get close to the pope.

And he also joked about it.

“The nice thing about Peruvians, including the person who with a lot of faith simply wanted to offer me a rosary, are things you carry in your heart – or maybe in your eye – but that mark the life of someone,” he said.

“It tells you that here truly there is enthusiasm. Here there is profound faith. Here there is a desire to receive the blessing of the Lord,” he said.

People often toss rosaries, stuffed animals, sports jerseys and other items toward the pope when he is in the popemobile and he has often wowed crowds with his quick reflexes and ability to catch them. His bodyguards, however, say these tossed items are some of their biggest security concerns when he’s out in public.

The post Pope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in Peru appeared first on Crux .
items.t: Pope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in Peru

items.title: Catholic ministry supports people of different faiths in Muslim-majority Malaysia
items.summary:
KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia — Noorzainny Luthfi was no stranger to hardship. Yet her family faced a new set of challenges when the COVID-19 pandemic hit Malaysia.

Her husband lost his job as a truck driver. The couple then struggled to provide for their three children in one of Kuala Lumpur’s low-income neighborhoods.

“We didn’t know what to do,” Noorzainny said. She now makes a living from a venture supported by the Catholic Church, which provides assistance to vulnerable communities regardless of their religious beliefs in Muslim-majority Malaysia.

Noorzainny’s husband came up with the idea of making piggy banks out of coconut shells. Friends and neighbors placed a few orders, and his hobby soon turned into a small business.

A year later, in 2022, a British friend suggested: What if you created a recycling program to turn waste into products you could sell? Following that advice, Noorzainny’s family founded Upcycled.

The connection with the church began after they set up a shop in their neighborhood. Catholic, Muslim and Hindu religious leaders visited the area from time to time to make donations to vulnerable people.

“The bishop saw our small factory and asked what we were doing,” Noorzainny said. “I told him we were collecting plastic, trying to educate kids and making products to support people in the community because most of them lost their jobs.”

A Catholic ministry extends its support across religious communities 

The Archdiocesan Office for Human Development in Kuala Lumpur is known as AOHD. It oversees 10 ministries that serve vulnerable communities. Among…

items.title: Kindness after the horrific destruction of an image of Jesus
items.summary:
Watching a man laughing as he breaks the arm off a statue of Jesus is shocking enough. But seeing the figure fall to the pavement and shatter, while the men responsible appear to find the whole episode hilarious, feels almost physically painful. Whatever your religious beliefs, it’s difficult to understand how anyone could find such disrespect amusing, particularly when the object in question means so much to so many people. Yet this was the scene captured on CCTV in Vilnius, Lithuania, on November 11, when two men removed the corpus from a crucifix outside the Shrine of Divine Mercy. As one carried the figure away, its arms were damaged before it fell and broke into pieces. The men then fled, leaving the shattered image on the pavement. The footage has understandably prompted outrage across the world, including from people who don’t share the Catholic faith. For Catholics, the location makes the incident especially distressing. items.title: Peru gave Leo the 1st book printed in S. America, with a personal touch
items.summary:
As Pope Leo XIV concluded his visit to Peru, the country’s National Library gave him a gift that managed to be historically significant and deeply personal at once: a facsimile edition of the Doctrina Christiana y Catecismo para Instrucción de los Indios, printed in Lima in 1584 — the first book ever printed in Peru and in all of South America. The Pope signed a copy, which will be preserved in the Library’s repositories as a record of the encounter. Leo XIV left Peru on November 16, the final day of a 12-day apostolic journey through Uruguay, Argentina, and his adopted homeland. The Doctrina Christiana of 1584 is not some historical curiosity. It was a deliberate act of innovative pastoral imagination, produced under the direction of Saint Turibius of Mogrovejo, the second Archbishop of Lima, as a tool for evangelizing the indigenous populations of the Andes. Written in three languages — Spanish, Quechua, and Aymara Read More…

Among the first royalty to follow in the footsteps of St. Francis in this way was St. Elizabeth of Hungary, daughter of the king of Hungary. items.title: Pope says he leaves Peru with what he always admired
items.summary:
“I came to proclaim Christ to you, and I leave with the witness of the faith and devotion that I always admired in you,” Pope Leo said, as he said farewell to his second homeland after an intense 12-day journey through South America. The Holy Father’s plane took off around 2:30 p.m. local time, and he has a flight home of more than 14 hours. He’s set to arrive at Rome’s Fiumicino Airport on Tuesday, November 17, at 10:25 a.m. “I have felt at home, and you have reminded me that the Church truly is a family,” Pope Leo reflected. “It was here,” he said, “that you taught me how to be a Bishop, and this time I learned a little more about serving as the Successor of Peter.”

items.title: Pope bids ‘hasta luego’ to his second homeland of Peru as he wraps up marathon South American trip
items.summary:
LIMA, Peru — Pope Leo XIV bid farewell to his beloved second homeland of Peru on Monday with an “hasta luego,” after a marathon 12-day South American tour that tested his stamina after lung cancer surgery.

Leo emerged from the Vatican’s residence in Lima to kick off his final morning, visiting a home for the elderly that he tended to during the COVID-19 pandemic, before a huge Mass at an air base in the Peruvian capital that’s expected to draw up to 1 million people.

Speaking to the crowd outside the residence, Leo thanked Peruvians for having accompanied him on his trip.

“Have a good day, thank you very much, and until later!” he said.

A trip and pontificate modeled on a missionary saint 

For the Chicago-born Leo, who spent two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop, the trip was an emotional homecoming to a place that he has credited with teaching him how to be a shepherd. Upon arrival, he declared that Peru was his “patria” or homeland, and he sang the national anthem alongside President Keiko Fujimori. Leo has American and Peruvian citizenship.

Over the course of the trip, it became clear that Leo modeled his ministry in Peru and now for the universal Catholic Church on the figure of the first archbishop of Lima, St. Turibius of Mogrovejo.

Mogrovejo, who lived from 1538-1606, is revered for having denounced abuses against Indigenous and enslaved people by Spanish colonizers. He is also remembered for having crisscrossed his vast diocese on foot and horseback to minister to his flock, learning Quechua and Aymara to better preach to its Indigenous…
items.t: Pope bids ‘hasta luego’ to his second homeland of Peru as he wraps up marathon South American trip

items.title: Pope Leo helps Argentines embrace Francis, the pontiff who once divided them
items.summary:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina — Vast crowds of young Argentines, a generation that Catholic leaders had feared was abandoning the pews, packed the parks of Buenos Aires and cheered as if at a concert when Pope Leo XIV promised a church open to “todos, todos, todos” — everyone, everyone, everyone.

Those words, like all of Leo’s surest applause lines during the visit, belonged to his Argentine predecessor, Pope Francis. So did much of the week’s adulation.

Francis’s fierce defense of the downtrodden made him a moral voice abroad but long embroiled him in political fights at home — controversy that many believe deterred him from returning as pope. More than a year after his death, the more measured Leo made the homecoming Francis never could, carrying on his legacy and helping Argentines embrace their once-polarizing pope as a unifying national figure.

“It’s as though it has finally become clear that Francis left a very important legacy, not just for Argentina but for the universal church,” said Pablo Forni, a sociologist at Argentina’s national research council, Conicet. “Leo is reaping what Francis sowed.”

Billboards welcoming Leo bore Francis’s face. Pilgrims waved signs declaring “Francisco y León, un solo corazón” — Francis and Leo, one heart. Even libertarian President Javier Milei, who once insulted Francis as “the representative of evil on earth,” declared Francis “the most important Argentine in history” at Leo’s welcome ceremony, bringing a packed hall of his political allies and foes to its feet.

A pope caught in the divide 

As archbishop of Buenos Aires, Francis —…
items.t: Pope Leo helps Argentines embrace Francis, the pontiff who once divided them

items.title: A hidden cathedral floor emerges in Sudan, revealing one of the biggest medieval churches
items.summary:
CAIRO — Archaeologists have unearthed the original floor of a monumental medieval cathedral in northern Sudan that could be bigger than the White House, revealing the scale and architectural significance of one of Nubia’s most important Christian buildings.

A Polish-Sudanese mission earlier this month uncovered a staircase with 36-foot-high walls that led them to the original floor level of the Great Church of Jesus, probably the largest church in medieval Nubia, in Sudan’s ancient city of Old Dongola.

The church was first found in 2021, but much of it remains buried, with the staircase the only area where archaeologists managed to reach the floor.

“This was a building larger than the famous White House … and we are planning to excavate it,” said Artur Obłuski, head of the Sudanese-Polish archaeological mission.

He said it was the largest and most important church in medieval Makuria, one of three kingdoms that emerged along the middle reaches of the Nile River following the arrival of Christian missionaries in the sixth century. The church is in Old Dongola on the eastern bank of the Nile, about 100 miles southeast of modern-day Dongola. The city is known for its numerous ancient churches.

He likened the church to Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, built by the Byzantine Emperor Justinian in 537, saying that the Great Church of Jesus played a similar role in medieval Nubia and northeastern Africa through its spatial planning and construction techniques.

“In the history of architecture, certain buildings emerge that, to use a modern term, become trendsetters. Hagia Sophia in…
items.t: A hidden cathedral floor emerges in Sudan, revealing one of the biggest medieval churches

items.title: Pope in Peruvian rainforest demands justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting Amazon
items.summary:
PUCALLPA, Peru — Pope Leo XIV on Sunday demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon and backed efforts by Indigenous peoples to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging, illegal mining and the “insatiable thirst for domination.”

On the penultimate day of his South American odyssey, Leo traveled into the Peruvian Amazon and channeled one of Pope Francis ’s core teachings that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.

“The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable,” Leo told Indigenous representatives and missionaries gathered along the Ucayali River in the northeastern city of Pucallpa.

He said he came to Pucallpa to support them in their search for justice and peace and referred to what environmental groups estimate have been 57 murders of environmental defenders between 2010-2024.

“The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice,” Leo said to applause from the crowd, many of whom were wearing traditional feathered headwear and face markings of the region.

Illegal mining ravaging the rainforest and driving Indigenous out 

In addition to the decades-long problem of deforestation, illegal gold mining has become an increasingly lucrative business in the Amazon, devastating forests and polluting rivers. Miners use makeshift suction dredges and mercury, a toxic metal, to extract gold.

Raphael Hoetmer, Western Amazon program director at Amazon Watch, said wars and conflicts around the world have driven up the price of gold, increasing demand that in turn is resulting in more…
items.t: Pope in Peruvian rainforest demands justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting Amazon

Under a clear blue sky, thousands of pro-life demonstrators marched through the city center of The Hague on November 14. Organizers reported a record 15,000 people took part and many participants said the crowd looked noticeably larger than last year. The march began at the Malieveld, a large grassy park, a 15-minute walk away from the Dutch Parliament. items.title: Leo XIV in Cusco: defending the sick and honoring local faith
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV spent November 15 in Cusco, the ancient capital of the Inca empire at 3,400 meters above sea level, in what became a sustained reflection on two themes: the dignity of the sick, and the value of the religious traditions that ordinary people build from their own faith. He was welcomed into the city by 500,000 people who lined seven kilometers of streets in the rain. His first stop was the archaeological park of Saqsayhuamán, where he met 100,000 faithful and representatives of local traditions amid the colossal stone ramparts of the ancient Inca fortress. His second was the Cathedral of the Virgen de la Asunción, built over the foundations of an Inca palace in the 17th and 18th centuries, where he prayed the Angelus alongside the sick, priests, and consecrated persons of the region. On the cathedral square, Leo addressed those suffering in body and soul. “In the eyes of the world, Read More…

items.title: The Pope has a Peruvian ID, with his Chiclayo address
items.summary:
It is not every day that a pope has a national identity card. Leo XIV does — and earlier this year, four RENIEC registrars traveled to the Vatican to update his data for a new electronic DNI 3.0, according to Peru’s state news agency Andina. He asked that his address remain registered in Chiclayo, the northern diocese where he served as bishop for nine years — a small but telling gesture from a man who has said throughout this trip that Peru is home. The DNIe 3.0 is Peru’s most secure identity document to date, launched in April 2025 and equipped with 64 security features — four times more than its predecessor. It does not expire. Robert Francis Prevost Martínez first obtained Peruvian nationality and his initial DNI in 2015, while serving as Bishop of Chiclayo. Leo XIV’s name appeared on the Chiclayo electoral roll for Peru’s regional and municipal elections held on October 4, Read More…

Considering his young age, Ledger, who hails from Virginia, has managed to do something pretty impressive: help police officers, firefighters, and paramedics better care for children with autism during emergencies. items.title: Blessed Solanus Casey’s unique connection to Peru
items.summary:
Blessed Solanus Casey’s birth name was Bernard Francis Casey, and he was affectionately called Barney by his family and friends. It wasn’t until he joined the Franciscan Order that he received the name Solanus. It’s an intriguing name, one few people have ever heard of and hardly anyone names their kids Solanus! What’s even more fascinating is how Bl. Solanus was given this name to honor a Franciscan missionary in Peru. St. Francis Solanus was born in Spain in the 16th century and was received into the Franciscan Order when he was 20 years old. He was eventually ordained and then sent to a friary to be the master of novices. After that assignment he was sent to South America, destined to be an influential missionary in a variety of countries. items.title: One of the secrets to a happy marriage

We’ve been married for almost 25 years now and she knows what I like. I like coffee. As I said, it’s a small thing, a simple gesture, but it isn’t really about the drink; it’s an act of kindness that unveils a hugely important reason that our marriage continues to thrive — she’s thinking of me even within the ordinary details of her life. items.title: How do we face uncertainty without allowing it to overwhelm us? This Islamic teaching shows us the way
items.summary:
For generations of Muslims, tawakkul has been an essential part of faith – making a sincere effort while recognising the limits of human control

I once asked an elderly naan seller on the streets of Kabul how he was managing to make a living. It was almost midday and he had not sold a single naan. What would he take home, I asked. “Tawakkul ba Khuda,” he replied.

He had a long silver beard, deep brown eyes and a beautiful smile. As a frontline journalist covering the Afghan war, I had heard those words many times before. From a young woman trying to establish a clothing business in the middle of the conflict, to a military commander confronting a deadly insurgency, to a school student preparing for the long and uncertain journey towards a university degree, the expression seemed to surface wherever hope and hardship met.

items.title: The reason we barely know who built the Gothic cathedrals
items.summary:
Walk into Chartres Cathedral and you are surrounded, by any measure, by one of the supreme achievements of human civilization. The light through the rose windows, the geometry of the vaulting, the carved figures on the Royal Portal, each one a minor miracle of stone. The whole building went up in roughly 26 years, after a fire destroyed the earlier structure in 1194 — an extraordinary speed for a structure of that complexity and scale. We know who ordered it built. Bishop Renaud de Mousson commissioned the reconstruction. The donors who funded the stained glass are also documented: the bakers, the fur merchants, the drapers, each guild immortalized in a panel depicting their trade alongside the saint they venerated. Their names and professions are there in the glass, permanent advertisements for piety and money. The people who actually built it — the master mason who solved the structural problems, the imagiers who carved the portal Read More… 

The reason we barely know who built the Gothic cathedrals

items.title: Who was the first Augustinian missionary in Peru?
items.summary:
It is well known that Pope Leo XIV, an Augustinian, spent much of his priestly ministry serving the people of Peru. Initially he served in a variety of capacities before being named the Bishop of Chiclayo in 2015. Pope Leo spent so much time in the country that he was able to become a naturalized citizen of Peru. The country holds a special place in his heart and is his “second home.” However Pope Leo, as Fr. Robert Provost, was assigned to Peru because of a long history of Augustinians serving in the South American country. Initially it was Dominican missionaries who brought Christianity to Peru in 1534, establishing a strong presence in the region. This is one of the reasons why two of Peru’s best known saints, St. Rose Lima and St. Martin de Porres, were Dominicans.
